passage: You want the honest version? Fine. I'm Aadhya. After graduation I applied to sixty jobs in four months. Most never replied. Twelve rejected me. Two interviews went badly. I'd cry in the bathroom so my parents wouldn't hear. My friend Vaibhav was in the same place, and we started a rule: every rejection, we'd text each other one thing to try differently. Like, "Shorter answers." Or, "Research the company first." Some days I didn't want to send anything. Some days I was angry at everyone who got hired. But slowly, my interviews got better. On the sixty-first try, I got an offer. It wasn't my dream job. But I learned I could keep going when it felt pointless.

qa.q: How many jobs did Aadhya apply to in four months?
qa.a: Aadhya applied to sixty jobs.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya cry in the bathroom?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and hopeless after so many rejections and wanted to hide that pain from the parents at home.

qa.q: What made Aadhya and Vaibhav's rule helpful?
qa.a: Turning each rejection into one lesson helped them learn and improve rather than just feel defeated.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel when Aadhya got the offer?
qa.a: Vaibhav would probably feel happy for Aadhya, and perhaps hopeful about the search still going on for Vaibhav. 🎉

grounding: A young adult describes absorbing repeated job rejections, learning from them and continuing.

passage: I'm Nitin, and Amandeep has been my friend since school. After college, he applied for government jobs. He failed the first exam by a few marks. Then the second. I saw him at the tea stall after the second result, stirring his tea for a long time without drinking it. He said, "Maybe I'm not made for this." I didn't know what to say. A week later, he was back at the library. He'd made a list of the topics he'd lost marks on. He joined a study group and practised old papers. He still had bad days. On the third try, he cleared the exam. I don't know how he kept going, but he told me, "Each fail showed me exactly where I was weak."

qa.q: What did Amandeep make a list of?
qa.a: He made a list of the topics he had lost marks on.

qa.q: What does Amandeep stirring his tea without drinking it suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was lost in disappointment and discouragement after failing again.

qa.q: What helped Amandeep continue after rejection?
qa.a: He used each failure to find his weak topics, joined a study group and practised old papers.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel watching Amandeep clear the exam?
qa.a: He'd likely feel relieved and proud of his friend's persistence.

grounding: A friend observes a young man absorbing repeated exam failures, learning from them and continuing.

March: He applied everywhere. Rejection emails piled up. One interviewer said he lacked experience. Raghav was angry and stayed in bed one whole day. Then he asked for feedback and got some.

May: He took a short course, built a small project, and updated his resume. The rejections still came. But one company invited him for a second round. He was nervous, but he prepared. He got the job. On the day he joined, he texted Karthik: "Dosa's on me tonight."

passage: Ujjwal, you've had nine rejections and you're ready to quit? Beta, at twenty-two I had thirty-one. I kept the letters in a shoebox, don't laugh. After the twelfth I sat on the terrace in Bhopal and cried, sure there was something wrong with me. My elder brother read a few and said, 'Look, Parveen, three of them mention the same thing: no practical experience.' That changed the question. It wasn't 'what's wrong with me', it was 'what's missing'. So I did an unpaid stint at a small accounts firm for three months while I kept applying. Some rejections still came with no reason at all, and those I simply had to let go. Number thirty-two said yes. Keep a shoebox, Ujjwal. Read it for patterns, not for proof you're useless.

qa.q: How many rejections did Parveen have at twenty-two?
qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel after the twelfth rejection?
qa.a: Parveen felt hopeless and upset, sure something was wrong with them, and cried on the terrace.

qa.q: What does Parveen suggest Ujjwal do with his rejections?
qa.a: Look for patterns to find what is missing and work on it, while letting go of rejections that give no reason.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel hearing Parveen's story?

passage: The rejection email arrived on the bus, while Seema was counting how many weeks her savings could cover rent in the shared flat in Thiruvananthapuram. Five, maybe six. 'We have decided to move forward with other candidates.' It was her fourth this month. She got off two stops early and walked in the drizzle, letting herself feel it. That evening Jomon, her flatmate, made black tea and asked, 'Did they say anything useful?' They hadn't. So she wrote back, politely asking for any feedback. Meanwhile she took a weekend shift at a bookshop café to stretch her money, and applied to two more roles that night, tweaking her cover letter for each. Two days later one recruiter replied: her portfolio was strong, but they wanted more client experience. It stung. It also gave her something to work on.

qa.q: How many rejections had Seema received that month?
qa.a: This was her fourth that month.

qa.q: Why did Seema get off the bus two stops early?
qa.a: She needed space to feel the disappointment privately, walking in the drizzle instead of pretending she was fine.

qa.q: Which of Seema's steps helped her keep going?
qa.a: Asking politely for feedback, taking a weekend shift to ease money worries, and continuing to apply with tailored cover letters.

qa.q: How might Jomon see his part that evening?
qa.a: He may have felt he could not fix things, but tea and one practical question helped her move from hurt to next steps.

grounding: Shows a graduate absorbing repeated rejection under money pressure, seeking feedback and continuing to apply.

passage: The fourteenth rejection email arrived while Ishita was on the local train from Andheri. "After careful consideration…" She read it twice, then put the phone away and watched the backs of buildings go past. At home Francis, her flatmate, was frying eggs. "Another?" "Fourteen." He slid a plate across. "Want to throw something or look at it?" She laughed despite herself. After dinner she opened the spreadsheet she had started at rejection five: company, role, stage reached, what they said. Francis leaned over. "You get past the written test every time. You drop at the case interview." She stared. Fourteen emails had felt like fourteen verdicts on her. The sheet said something narrower: one skill to fix. She booked a free case-practice session at the alumni cell for Saturday, then sent the next application before bed.

qa.q: Where was Ishita when the fourteenth rejection arrived?
qa.a: On the local train from Andheri.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she watched the buildings go past?
qa.a: Ishita felt discouraged and hurt, as though each rejection were a verdict on her.

qa.q: What did the spreadsheet reveal, and why does that help?
qa.a: She passes the written test but drops at the case interview, so she can practise one skill instead of doubting everything.

qa.q: How does Francis see Ishita's rejections?
qa.a: Francis stays calm and practical, seeing a pattern to fix rather than a failure, and supports her with food and humour.

grounding: After fourteen rejections, a young woman in Mumbai uses a log to find what to fix and keeps applying.

passage:
"They picked the other candidate." Jomon dropped his bag by the door. "Final round. I was so sure."
Arohi muted the TV. "Chetta. Come, sit."
"Third final round this year, Arohi. Third."
"Did they say why?"
"Some line about 'a stronger fit'."
"Did you ask them what that meant?"
He stared at her. "You can ask?"
"Of course. Politely. My friend Shilpa did, and the recruiter told her exactly which answer lost it."
Jomon rubbed his eyes. "What if they say I was terrible?"
"Then you'll know. Right now you're guessing, and your guesses are worse than anything they'd say."
He was quiet. Then: "I'll write tonight. Short. Thank them, ask for one piece of feedback."
"And tomorrow you apply to the Kochi one you bookmarked."
"You're bossy."
"I'm your little sister. It's my job."

qa.q: Which round did Jomon reach?
qa.a: The final round.

qa.q: What was Jomon worried about in asking for feedback?
qa.a: Jomon was anxious that they might say he was terrible, after three final-round rejections this year.

qa.q: Why is asking for one piece of feedback a good next step?
qa.a: It replaces painful guessing with real information he can use, and a short, polite email keeps the door open.

qa.q: How does Arohi see her brother's rejection?
qa.a: Arohi sees it as frustrating but fixable, and gently pushes him to act instead of spiralling.

grounding: A young man rejected at a third final round is nudged by his sister to seek feedback and keep applying.

passage: My name's Lokesh, and for eight months after graduation every conversation at home began with "Any news?" No. By month seven: thirty applications, four interviews, zero offers. Relatives stopped asking me and started asking my father, which was worse. Around month five I took a temporary data-entry job at a transport office, mostly to stop feeling useless. I was embarrassed to tell my friend Vaibhav, who had been placed on campus. When I did, he said, "So you're learning how a real logistics office works. Put that on your resume." I hadn't seen it that way. I started noticing how the office tracked trucks, and suggested a simpler sheet. My supervisor adopted it. In month eight, an interviewer at a logistics firm spent twenty minutes asking about that sheet. I got the job. Those months of rejection still sting. They also taught me what to say.

qa.q: What temporary job did Lokesh take?
qa.a: A data-entry job at a transport office.

qa.q: Why was Lokesh embarrassed to tell Vaibhav about the job?
qa.a: Lokesh felt embarrassed because Vaibhav had been placed on campus, and the temporary job felt like proof of failing.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's reframe change what Lokesh did next?
qa.a: Seeing the job as learning how a logistics office works led Lokesh to improve the tracking sheet, which became the story that won the interview.

qa.q: What was it like for Lokesh's father when relatives started asking him?
qa.a: The father was probably uncomfortable and worried, carrying other people's questions about his child's future.

grounding: A graduate looks back on months of rejection and uncertainty, and how a temporary job became the way forward.

Career centre adviser's note.
Naveen, final year, came in today with a list of fourteen rejection emails. He said, "Maybe I'm just not good enough."
We went through them. Nine never gave feedback. Three said his technical round was strong but his communication weak. Two roles weren't a fit for his skills anyway.
I pointed out the pattern. He nodded slowly. "So it's not everything. It's one thing."
We booked three mock interviews focused on explaining his projects clearly. His friend Nikita, who got placed last month, offered to practise with him too.
He left looking tired, but less defeated. Follow-up in two weeks. — Mr Bose

passage:
From his small town in Bundelkhand, Ramesh applied to thirty-one jobs in four months after his BCom. He got four interviews and no offers. Each rejection email felt like a door closing on his whole family's hopes.
One evening his younger brother Divyansh found him staring at the ceiling. "Show me the emails."
They read them together. Two companies had given reasons: "limited experience with accounting software" and "communication in English".
"That's not 'you're useless'," Divyansh said. "That's a list."
Ramesh joined a free accounting software course at the town library and started practising English interviews with Divyansh every night on the roof, even when they both felt silly.
Two more months, eleven more rejections. Then an offer from a firm in Jhansi. He framed the first rejection email as a joke. It still hung by his desk.

qa.q: How many jobs did Ramesh apply to in four months?
qa.a: Thirty-one jobs.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel about each rejection?
qa.a: Ramesh felt crushed and heavy, as if each rejection closed a door on his family's hopes.

qa.q: What turned rejection into something useful, and why?
qa.a: Reading the emails for reasons and turning them into a list of skills to build, because it gave him specific steps instead of despair.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt practising English with his brother on the roof?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt a bit silly but proud to help, and invested in Ramesh's success.

grounding: Shows a young adult absorbing repeated job rejections, learning from them and continuing until he succeeds.

passage:
In Johannesburg, Zanele had been rejected by every graduate programme she'd applied to: nine of them. The ninth email arrived while she was on a crowded minibus, and she had to look out the window so nobody saw her face.
That evening her friend Hana came over with vetkoek and sat on the floor with her. "What's the pattern?"
"I get to the final round and then nothing."
"So ask."
Zanele hated the idea. But she emailed two companies asking for feedback. One replied: strong skills, but her answers were too long and she didn't ask any questions at the end.
She laughed, a little bitterly. Then she practised with Hana: shorter answers, two good questions ready.
The tenth application went to final round too. This time she asked about their training. Two weeks later, she got an offer.

qa.q: How many graduate programmes had rejected Zanele?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: Why did Zanele look out the window on the minibus?
qa.a: Zanele felt hurt and embarrassed and didn't want anyone to see her face.

qa.q: What was the most useful thing Zanele did after the rejections?
qa.a: Asking for feedback, because it gave her a specific pattern, long answers and no questions, that she could fix.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt seeing her friend get the offer?
qa.a: Hana would probably feel happy and relieved, having sat with Zanele through the hard part.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult learning from repeated rejections by seeking feedback and continuing.

passage:
At the district employment office, Manoj waited for his appointment with Asif, the career counsellor, holding a folder of rejection letters. Eighteen in five months, for sales and office jobs.
"I'm thinking of giving up and going back to the village," Manoj said, very quietly.
Asif didn't rush him. "Before you decide, let's look at what these tell us."
They sorted the letters: nine never replied beyond the form, five said "not shortlisted", four came after interviews. "So you get interviews," Asif said. "That's something. What happens there?"
Manoj admitted he froze when asked about salary, and he'd been applying to anything, even jobs he didn't want.
They made a plan: apply to fewer, better-fit jobs; practise interviews at the centre every Wednesday; keep a list of what each rejection taught him.
Manoj still felt tired. But he walked out with a Wednesday appointment.

qa.q: How many rejection letters did Manoj have?
qa.a: Eighteen, in five months.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he spoke very quietly about giving up?
qa.a: Manoj felt discouraged and ashamed, worn down by the rejections.

qa.q: How did Asif help Manoj without dismissing his feelings?
qa.a: Asif listened, then sorted the letters to find patterns and made a practical plan with weekly practice, so Manoj could keep going.

qa.q: How might Asif see Manoj's situation?
qa.a: Asif seems to see real potential, since Manoj gets interviews, and wants to help him learn rather than give up.

grounding: Shows a young adult absorbing repeated job rejection, learning from it with a counsellor and continuing.

Dear Payal ma'am,
I wanted to tell you where things stand, since you asked me to write even if the news was bad. It was: twelve applications since graduation, nine silences, three rejections. The last one was the design studio I really wanted. I read the email on the bus and got off two stops early so no one would see my face.
I took your advice anyway. I asked them for feedback, politely, and they actually replied: strong visuals, but no explanation of my process. That stung, but it was fair. I've added short case notes to three projects and applied to four more places this week.
Some days I still wonder if I'm good enough. But I'm treating each no as information, not a verdict.
Thank you for not letting me hide.
Lavanya
